name: Sandia National Laboratories

profile.address: 880A, K South Avenue Southeast, Bernalillo County, New Mexico, 87116
profile.reading: This facility in Bernalillo County, New Mexico, is a high performance computing site operated by Sandia National Laboratories, whose main New Mexico campus sits on Kirtland Air Force Base in Albuquerque and employs more than 12,000 people. Sandia is a United States federal research laboratory, owned by the government but managed under contract, currently by National Technology and Engineering Solutions of Sandia, a wholly owned subsidiary of Honeywell International, a management contract that began in May 2017. It is one of three national laboratories run under the Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration, alongside Los Alamos and Lawrence Livermore, and its mission centers on nuclear weapons stewardship, nonproliferation, arms control support and broader national security science, work organized across multiple technical areas on the Kirtland site. Sandia's Center for Computing Research develops the computer system architecture, both hardware and software, along with the computational physical simulation and data and decision science capability that underpin this mission, describing its work as addressing some of the nation's most demanding national security computing challenges and explicitly referencing exascale class computing among its research goals. High performance computing at Sandia traces back through machines such as the ASCI Red system of the late 1990s, an early terascale computer built for the Accelerated Strategic Computing Initiative, through to more recent large scale systems the laboratory has fielded for stockpile stewardship simulation, weapons physics modeling and broader defense science computing. Because this work supports classified and sensitive national security missions, Sandia does not publish the kind of commercial specifications, such as leasable floor area or power capacity available to tenants, that describe a colocation data center. What is publicly documented is the laboratory's role, its ownership and management structure, and a general history of fielding some of the country's most capable government owned research computers in support of the Department of Energy's nuclear security mission, rather than any commercial hosting business. Facilities of this kind require electrical power and cooling infrastructure on a scale comparable to large commercial data centers simply to keep thousands of processors and accelerators running continuously, even though the laboratory does not publish those figures the way a commercial colocation provider would, since Sandia's computing is built to support its own mission rather than to be leased out, and detailed capacity numbers are treated as programmatic rather than public information.

reading: Sandia National Laboratories operates a Department of Energy and National Nuclear Security Administration research computing facility in Albuquerque, New Mexico, managed and operated by National Technology and Engineering Solutions of Sandia, LLC, a Honeywell subsidiary, under an NNSA management and operating contract. Sandia's public news releases have documented several notable supercomputing systems over the years, including Astra, an Arm-processor-based supercomputer prototype deployed in 2018 that was among the first large-scale Arm architecture systems to appear on the Top500 list of the world's fastest supercomputers, alongside other named systems referenced in Sandia coverage such as Antarctica and Stout. Sandia's primary mission is national security science and engineering in support of NNSA's nuclear weapons stewardship responsibilities, alongside broader computing, materials science, and engineering research. As with Oak Ridge National Laboratory and other Department of Energy national laboratories recorded in this registry, Sandia's facility serves a mixed classified and unclassified research mission rather than a commercial colocation function, and this registry does not estimate IT capacity in megawatts beyond what Sandia's own public news releases describe about specific named computing systems.
